literal: His son Sheng, styled Shixing, inherited the title and served as Supervisor of Palace Ushers.
idiomatic: His son Sheng, styled Shixing, inherited the fief and rose to Supervisor of Palace Ushers.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: Sheng's younger brother Shouxing, [8] was clever and fond of learning from youth.
idiomatic: Sheng's younger brother Shouxing, [8] was bright and bookish from boyhood.

literal: At the start of Emperor Shizong's reign he was made Regional Inspector of Xuzhou; in office he was greedy and cruel and lost the people's hearts.
idiomatic: Early in Emperor Shizong's reign he became inspector of Xuzhou; greedy and brutal in office, he lost the people.

literal: His cousin, Palace Attendant Hui, deeply resented his ability and slandered him to the emperor; an edict ordered Master of Writing Cui Liang to ride post-horses and investigate.
idiomatic: His cousin Palace Attendant Hui, who envied his talent, denounced him to the throne; Cui Liang of the Masters of Writing was ordered to investigate by express relay.

literal: The day Liang set out he took Hui's instructions and had three widows flogged until they falsely accused themselves, saying Shouxing had forced them to be his bondmaids.
idiomatic: On the day he departed Liang followed Hui's orders, had three widows beaten until they confessed that Shouxing had pressed them into servitude.

literal: Shouxing, fearing he could not escape, had his wife's younger brother, Army Staff Officer Xue Xiuyi, bring ten carts hauling wheat past his place of detention.
idiomatic: Convinced he would not escape, Shouxing had his brother-in-law Xue Xiuyi, a staff officer, drive ten carts of wheat past the compound where he was held.

literal: Shouxing climbed over the wall and got out.
idiomatic: Shouxing scaled the wall and fled.

literal: Xiuyi put Shouxing in a great wooden chest, heaped wheat on top, and hauled him away.
idiomatic: Xiuyi hid him in a great wooden chest, piled wheat on top, and drove him out.

literal: He reached Hedong and hid in Xiuyi's house.
idiomatic: He reached Hedong and lay hidden in Xiuyi's home.

literal: When an amnesty was proclaimed he came out to see Emperor Shizong, confessed that Hui had slandered him, and the emperor imposed no further penalty.
idiomatic: After an amnesty he appeared before Shizong, said Hui had framed him, and was not punished further.

literal: Earlier, when Shouxing was Junior Mentor to the Heir Apparent, Wang Xian was in the Eastern Palace in a low station; on official business Shouxing had him beaten thirty strokes.
idiomatic: Once, while Shouxing served as junior mentor in the Eastern Palace, Wang Xian held a low post; on official grounds Shouxing had him thrashed thirty strokes.

literal: When Xian won favor and became Censor-in-Chief, he memorialized that Shouxing at home often murmured complaints and slandered the court.
idiomatic: When Xian grew powerful as Censor-in-Chief, he reported that Shouxing grumbled at home and reviled the court.

literal: Because the emperor was deep in drink and unaware, he submitted the matter, had the emperor write "approved," and sent it straight to Shouxing ordering him to die.
idiomatic: The emperor was drunk and unheeding; Xian submitted the charge, had him scrawl approval, and sent the order straight to Shouxing to die.

literal: The emperor's hand formed only half the characters; those present knew it was not his true will, but they feared Hui's power and dared not speak up.
idiomatic: The emperor's characters were half-formed; witnesses knew his heart was not in it, yet they feared Hui and dared not intervene.

literal: On the day of execution Xian went in person to watch.
idiomatic: On the day of execution Xian went to watch in person.

literal: Shouxing ordered brush and wrote his own epitaph: "A man of Luoyang, surname Yuan, given name Jing—virtue without its season, his years not long."
idiomatic: Shouxing called for brush and ink and wrote his own epitaph: "A man of Luoyang, surname Yuan, given name Jing—virtue without its hour, years cut short."

literal: " The rest of the text is mostly not recorded.
idiomatic: " The remainder is not fully recorded.

literal: He turned to his son and said, "Put a hundred sheets of paper and two brushes in my coffin—I mean to sue Xian in the underworld.
idiomatic: He told his son, "Lay a hundred sheets of paper and two brushes in my coffin. I intend to bring suit against Xian below."

literal: If Gaozu's spirit has knowledge, within a hundred days he will surely take Xian; if there is truly no knowledge, what is there to cling to?"
idiomatic: If Gaozu's spirit sees, he will take Xian within a hundred days; if the dead know nothing, why linger at all?"

literal: " When Emperor Shizong died, Xian was soon killed.
idiomatic: When Shizong died, Xian was killed soon after.

literal: As for Shouxing's death, opinion of the time also held that the former Censor-in-Chief's impeachment of Gao
idiomatic: When Shouxing died, contemporaries also blamed the former censor's impeachment of Gao

literal: 〈lacuna〉
idiomatic: 〈lacuna〉

literal: was what led to slander and brought the affair about.
idiomatic: for the slander that had set the tragedy in motion.

literal: When Empress Dowager Ling held court, Gentleman of the Three Excellencies Cui Hong memorialized to clear Shouxing; an edict posthumously exonerated him, made him posthumous Regional Inspector of Yuzhou, and gave the posthumous title Zhuang.
idiomatic: When Empress Dowager Ling ruled, Cui Hong of the Three Excellencies petitioned to clear him; the court posthumously exonerated him, made him inspector of Yuzhou, and styled him Zhuang.

literal: Shouxing's younger brother Yisheng died young.
idiomatic: His brother Yisheng died in youth.

literal: Zhong's younger brother De was enfeoffed as Duke of Hejian.
idiomatic: Zhong's brother De was made Duke of Hejian.

literal: He died while General Who Guards the South and was posthumously made Regional Inspector of Caozhou.
idiomatic: He died as General Who Guards the South and was posthumously made inspector of Caozhou.

literal: De's son Ti was Administrator of Yingchuan.
idiomatic: De's son Ti served as administrator of Yingchuan.

literal: He died as Regional Inspector of Guang Province; posthumous title Gong.
idiomatic: He died as inspector of Guang and was posthumously styled Gong.

literal: Zhong's son Hui, [11] styled Jingxi.
idiomatic: Zhong's son Hui, [11] styled Jingxi.

literal: From youth he was grave and keen and had some knowledge of letters and history.
idiomatic: As a youth he was grave and quick, with some learning in letters and history.

literal: When Emperor Shizong took the throne he was appointed Master of Writing, Director of Foreign Guests.
idiomatic: At Shizong's accession he became Director of Foreign Guests in the Masters of Writing.

literal: On a tour inspecting local customs he returned, reported to the throne to satisfaction, and was made Attendant Gentleman at the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: After touring local customs he reported to the throne to satisfaction and was made attendant gentleman at the Yellow Gate.

literal: At first, when Gaozu moved the capital to Luoyang, the old nobles in office all found relocation hard; to reconcile feelings the court then allowed winter residence in the south and summer in the north.
idiomatic: When Gaozu moved the capital to Luoyang, old nobles balked at relocation; to soothe them the court allowed winters in the south and summers in the north.

literal: Emperor Shizong was much swayed by attendants' words; outsiders then raised talk of returning north, even posting notices to sell fields and houses, unsettled in their dwellings.
idiomatic: Shizong heeded his attendants; rumor spread of a return north, notices went up to sell houses, and people could not settle.

literal: Hui then requested a private audience to speak on affairs.
idiomatic: Hui asked for a private audience.

literal: Emperor Shizong said, "When the late emperor moved the capital he planned winter south and summer north; I wish to follow that settled edict—hence outsiders' talk."
idiomatic: Shizong said, "When the late emperor moved the capital he meant winter south and summer north. I mean to keep that edict—hence the talk outside."

literal: Hui said, "The late emperor moved the capital because the people clung to their native soil; he issued the winter-summer dual residence edict only to ease their minds for the moment.
idiomatic: Hui answered, "The move was for people who clung to their soil; the dual-residence edict was only to calm them for a time.

literal: That was language for the moment, not the late emperor's true intent.
idiomatic: That was speech for the hour, not his true intent.

literal: Moreover, those who came north have dwelt in peace many years; public and private plans are set—there is no thought of return.
idiomatic: Those who came north have lived here for years; households and offices are settled—no one wishes to return.

literal: Your Majesty should complete Gaozu's work of fixing the tripod—do not trust wicked ministers' contrary talk."
idiomatic: Finish Gaozu's work of fixing the capital. Do not heed wicked ministers who say otherwise."

literal: " The emperor followed this.
idiomatic: Shizong took his counsel.

literal: He was promoted again to Palace Attendant and concurrent General of the Right Guard; though he brought no real benefit, he was deeply favored.
idiomatic: He rose again to palace attendant and general of the right guard; though he did little good, favor ran deep.

literal: Whatever secret matters arose within the forbidden precinct, Hui alone received orders and stored them in a cabinet—only when Hui entered was it opened; none of the other attendants or yellow-gate officers knew.
idiomatic: Secret business of the inner palace went into a cabinet on Hui's orders alone; only he could open it—other attendants and yellow-gate officers knew nothing.

literal: Palace Attendant Lu Chang also received favoring glances, so people of the time called them "the starving-tiger general and the hungry-eagle attendant."
idiomatic: Palace Attendant Lu Chang shared the favor, and people nicknamed them "the starving-tiger general and the hungry-eagle attendant."

literal: He was moved to Minister of the Imperial Secretariat; selling offices for bribes had fixed prices—great commanderies two thousand bolts, middling one thousand, lesser five hundred; other posts had their own scales; the realm called it the "market bureau."
idiomatic: As minister of the imperial secretariat he sold offices at fixed rates—two thousand bolts for a great commandery, one thousand for a middling, five hundred for a lesser—and the realm called his ministry the market bureau.

literal: Sent out as Regional Inspector of Jizhou, the day he left his post a train of carts loaded goods from Xindu to Tangyin without break along the road.
idiomatic: Made inspector of Jizhou, he left office with carts in an unbroken line from Xindu to Tangyin.

literal: When a cart lacked grease or horn, he cut horns live from any ox met on the road to supply the need.
idiomatic: When carts lacked grease or horn fittings, his men cut horns from oxen met on the road.

literal: Hui audited registered households, allowed self-report of heads, and levied fifty thousand bolts of silk in tax.
idiomatic: He audited household registers, allowed self-report of dependents, and levied fifty thousand bolts of silk.

literal: Yet his exactions knew no limit and the people suffered.
idiomatic: Yet his levies never ceased, and the people groaned under them.

literal: At the start of Emperor Suzong's reign he was summoned as Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing and ordered to handle Secretariat selection affairs.
idiomatic: At Suzong's accession he was recalled as left vice director of the Masters of Writing and told to handle personnel selection.

literal: He memorialized: "I have heard that the root of governing men lies in entrusting prefects and governors.
idiomatic: He submitted: "The root of rule lies in prefects and governors.

literal: With the right talent, government is level and things are ordered; with the wrong men, lawsuits rise and resentment knots.
idiomatic: Find the right men and government runs level; choose wrongly and suits multiply and resentment knots.

literal: Unless one inspects good and evil and clearly rewards or punishes, how will one dismiss the greedy and idle and advance the pure and diligent?
idiomatic: Without inspection and clear reward and punishment, how dismiss the greedy and raise the diligent?

literal: I venture that grand envoys on inspection tours must broaden costs of welcome and send-off;
idiomatic: Grand inspection envoys widen welcome and send-off costs;

literal: censors who ride post to impeach often bend authority into abusive punishment.
idiomatic: censors who ride post to impeach often bend authority into abusive punishment.

literal: Moreover, brief comings and goings cannot grasp matters fully; even when there are selections and recommendations, they are often not fair.
idiomatic: Brief tours cannot grasp affairs fully; even when names are raised, justice is uneven.

literal: I think the Three Excellencies, the Eight Seats, attendants, and yellow-gate officers should each set out eyes and ears, inquire abroad into how provincial and garrison governors, military commanders, and magistrates govern men, and whether prefects and county chiefs are capable.
idiomatic: Let the Three Excellencies, Eight Seats, attendants, and yellow-gate officers each set eyes and ears abroad to learn how governors, commanders, and magistrates rule.

literal: If moral teaching is well ordered and purity stands alone, they should be named and promptly promoted.
idiomatic: Where teaching is sound and conduct pure, name them and promote them at once.

literal: If governing achievement is void and greed or cruelty is heard from afar, show the document and register demotion or dismissal.
idiomatic: Where rule fails or greed and cruelty travel far, publish the order and demote or dismiss.

literal: Thus without leaving the court hall one would sit knowing the four quarters—dignified, hands folded, with clear reward and careful punishment."
idiomatic: Then without leaving the hall you would know the realm—seated in dignity, with reward clear and punishment measured."

literal: He also submitted that "the censor's office is fit for hawks and falcons—they must bare claw and fang and seize something to tear.
idiomatic: He also wrote that censors are hawks and falcons—they must bare claw and seize prey.

literal: If one chooses young men fresh in blood and vigor, I fear their rash forthrightness will wound widely.
idiomatic: Choose hot-blooded youths and they will wound too widely.

literal: I think one should choose veteran officials experienced in affairs, loyal, steady, and even-tempered."
idiomatic: Choose seasoned officials who are loyal, steady, and even-tempered."

literal: " An edict sent this outside and ordered implementation accordingly.
idiomatic: An edict sent the plan out for implementation.

literal: Later an edict had Hui, with Prince of Rencheng Cheng, Prince of Jingzhao Yu, and Prince of Dongping Kuang, jointly decide great affairs of the Gate Department.
idiomatic: Later Hui was ordered, with Prince Cheng of Rencheng, Prince Yu of Jingzhao, and Prince Kuang of Dongping, to decide great Gate Department affairs together.

literal: Hui again submitted a letter on governing essentials: "First: the censor's office must obtain worthy men—must get the right person, not bound by rank and grade, long in the post, held to success.
idiomatic: Hui wrote again on essentials of rule: "First, censors must obtain worthy men—the right person, not bound by rank, long in post, held to results.

literal: Second: settle the people and quiet the borders, act as times require. Lately frontier generals have lost far-reaching strategy and grasp at one-in-ten-thousand gains; the good will of Chu and Liang is unheard of, while silkworm-wives' grievances knot again and again—this is what mediocrities do, keen for illicit profit.
idiomatic: Second, settle people and quiet borders and move as times require. Frontier generals lately grasp at trifling gains; goodwill with Chu and Liang is unheard of while silkworm-wives' grievances knot again—mediocrities keen for illicit profit.

literal: The plan to pacify Wu has its own good design—not in one city or one garrison.
idiomatic: The plan to pacify Wu has its own design—not in one city or one garrison.

literal: Moreover, several Hebei provinces are the state's foundation; famine has run many years and households have scattered.
idiomatic: Several Hebei provinces are the state's foundation; famine has run for years and households have scattered.

literal: Now troops on the borders are levied again—even on a day like this, how easy is any move?
idiomatic: Troops on the borders are levied again—even today, how easy is any move?

literal: I think that for several years one should only quiet the borders to cease corvée and garrison duty, settle the people and encourage farming, and show grace to this central realm.
idiomatic: For years the sole policy should be quiet borders, end corvée and garrison duty, settle people, encourage farming, and show grace to the central realm.

literal: I ask a stern order to frontier generals: from now on, when bandit garrisons seek to submit inward, do not rashly send relief or receive them—all must be reported; violators, though they have merit, should be judged by violation of edict.
idiomatic: Order frontier generals: when enemy garrisons seek to submit, do not receive them without memorial—violators judged by edict even if they have merit.

literal: Third: the state's stores rely only on Hebei.
idiomatic: Third, the state's stores rely only on Hebei.

literal: Famine piled year on year; households fled and scattered; fraud grew and bred concealment—shrinking the old and young in the rolls, falsely registering deaths and losses.
idiomatic: Famine piled up; households fled; fraud bred concealment—shrinking dependents on the rolls and falsely registering deaths.

literal: Collecting men's land tax and labor levy, they cut portions into their own pockets.
idiomatic: Tax and labor dues were cut into private pockets.

literal: The people suffer below; the government loses above.
idiomatic: The people suffered below; the treasury lost above.

literal: Unless new flexible rules are set and inspection applied well, the drain will not soon end.
idiomatic: Unless new rules and strict inspection are set, the drain will not end.

literal: I ask that this be debated and the articles clearly proclaimed."
idiomatic: Debate this and proclaim the articles clearly."

literal: " The emperor accepted it.
idiomatic: The emperor accepted it.

literal: Chenliu Wang Qian was a son of Heggen, son of Emperor Zhaocheng.
idiomatic: Qian, Prince of Chenliu, was son of Heggen, son of Emperor Zhaocheng.

literal: From youth he was known for strength and courage.
idiomatic: From youth he was famed for strength and courage.

literal: At the start of the Dengguo era he was granted the title Duke of Chenliu.
idiomatic: At the start of Dengguo he was made Duke of Chenliu.

literal: With Prince Wei Yi he broke the Chufu tribe.
idiomatic: With Prince Wei Yi he broke the Chufu tribe.

literal: He followed in the attack on Wei Chen.
idiomatic: He followed the attack on Wei Chen.

literal: When Murong Bao came to raid, Qian cut off his left wing.
idiomatic: When Murong Bao raided, Qian cut off his left wing.

literal: Bao was defeated; Chui came in rage and resentment to Sanggan.
idiomatic: Bao was beaten; Chui came to Sanggan in rage.

literal: Qian was brave but slighted the enemy and fell in battle in the field.
idiomatic: Brave but heedless, Qian fell in the field.

literal: Yue was outwardly harmonious and inwardly crafty.
idiomatic: Yue was smooth outside and treacherous within.

literal: Taizu, because Prince Huan had died in the king's service, gave him special favor and intimacy.
idiomatic: Because Prince Huan had died in royal service, Taizu favored him with special intimacy.

literal: He became General of the Left and inherited the fief.
idiomatic: He became general of the left and inherited the title.

literal: Later he was made Imperial Clan Mentor.
idiomatic: Later he was made imperial clan mentor.

literal: Yue relied on favor and was proud; he often told intimates such as Wang Luosheng, "Once the imperial carriage halts forever, I need only yield to the Duke of Wei—who else would stand before me?"
idiomatic: Proud in favor, he told intimates such as Wang Luosheng, "When the throne falls vacant I yield only to the Duke of Wei—who else stands before me?"

literal: " Prince Wei Yi had a fine beard and was respected within and without—hence Yue's words.
idiomatic: Prince Wei Yi wore a fine beard and was revered within and without—hence the remark.

literal: At first, when Yao Xing ransomed Di Bozhi, Yue escorted him; the route passed Yanmen, and Yue secretly won over local strongmen behind their backs to curry favor.
idiomatic: When Yao Xing ransomed Di Bozhi, Yue escorted him through Yanmen and secretly won over local strongmen.

literal: Later, when he was rebuked for an affair, he fled to Yanmen, plotted to gather heroes and attempt sedition, was seized by locals and sent in; Taizu pardoned and did not punish.
idiomatic: Rebuked later, he fled to Yanmen to gather heroes for sedition; locals seized him and sent him in; Taizu pardoned him.

literal: When Emperor Taizong took the throne he brought Yue in to attend court; Yue still harbored treacherous designs and told the emperor, "The mixed people of the capital cannot be trusted—those not of our kind should be killed.
idiomatic: Taizong brought him to court; Yue still plotted and told him, "The mixed people of the capital cannot be trusted—kill those not of our kind.

literal: Moreover, the people of Yanmen are mostly deceitful—they too can all be killed."
idiomatic: The people of Yanmen are mostly deceitful—kill them as well."

literal: " He wished to settle private grudges.
idiomatic: He meant to settle private scores.
